headings.title: Introduction to Referencing and Citation
headings.content: Referencing and citation form the backbone of scholarly communication in nursing. When student nurses and researchers build clinical guidelines or write essays, they must anchor their claims in verifiable evidence. A **citation** is a shorthand marker placed within the body of a text to acknowledge the original creator of an idea, statistic, or direct quote. A **reference**, conversely, is the complete bibliographic entry compiled at the end of the document, providing all necessary details for a reader to locate the source independently. Neglecting this system blurs the line between personal clinical opinion and empirically tested fact, undermining the rigor required for evidence-based nursing practice across Nigeria and globally.

headings.title: Academic Integrity and Plagiarism Prevention
headings.content:
Academic integrity demands absolute honesty in the creation and presentation of scholarly work. In nursing, where patient safety rests on accurate information, sloppy scholarship can translate into dangerous clinical errors. **Plagiarism** occurs when someone takes another person's words, data, or concepts and passes them off as their own original creation. This ethical breach ranges from outright copying of an entire journal article to unintentional patchwriting—changing a few words in a sentence without altering the underlying structure or crediting the author. Maintaining integrity requires meticulous note-taking during literature reviews and a clear understanding of when and what to cite. Common forms of plagiarism include:

- **Global Plagiarism**: Submitting an entire document written by someone else as one's own.
- **Patchwriting**: Piecing together phrases from multiple sources with minimal changes to sentence structure.
- **Self-Plagiarism**: Reusing substantial portions of one's previously published or submitted coursework without proper disclosure.

headings.title: In-Text Citations versus Reference Lists
headings.content:
The relationship between in-text citations and the reference list is governed by a strict rule of correspondence: every source cited in the body must appear in the reference list, and every reference listed must have been cited at least once in the text. Personal communications, such as unrecorded verbal interviews or private clinical notes, are an exception because readers cannot retrieve them; these are cited only in-text.

| Feature | In-Text Citation | Reference List Entry |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Location** | Inside the paragraphs of the body text | At the very end of the research paper |
| **Detail Level** | Brief (author surname and publication year) | Comprehensive (author, year, title, publisher/journal, DOI) |
| **Primary Purpose** | Directs the reader immediately to the source | Provides full retrieval data for verification |

headings.title: Major Referencing Styles in Healthcare
headings.content:
Different academic journals and nursing institutions enforce distinct referencing styles. Selecting the correct style depends entirely on the publisher's guidelines or the academic department's handbook. 

1. **APA (American Psychological Association)**: Widely used in nursing, psychology, and social sciences. Emphasizes the author-date system (e.g., Adebayo, 2023), highlighting when the research was conducted.
2. **Vancouver Style**: Heavily utilized in biomedical journals and clinical medicine. Relies on a numeric system where citations appear as superscript numbers (e.g., Adebayo²) corresponding to an ordered reference list.
3. **Harvard Style**: Another author-date variant common across British and Commonwealth-influenced higher education institutions, bearing strong similarities to APA format.
4. **Chicago Manual of Style**: Frequently used in history and humanities, utilizing either footnotes and a bibliography or author-date formats.

headings.title: Formatting Citations for Various Sources in APA
headings.content: Applying APA style correctly requires attention to the specific format of the source material. A journal article citation looks vastly different from a book or an internet webpage. When citing a journal article, include the author, year, article title, journal name in italics, volume number, issue number, and page range, along with a Digital Object Identifier (DOI) when available. Books require the author, year, book title in italics, and publisher name. For web sources, incorporating the URL at the end of the reference is standard practice. When a work has three or more authors, modern APA guidelines streamline the in-text citation by naming only the first author followed by "et al." from the very first mention, saving space and improving readability in busy clinical research papers.

headings.title: Citation Management Tools
headings.content: Managing dozens or hundreds of references manually opens the door to formatting errors and misplaced bibliographic data. Reference management software—such as Zotero, Mendeley, or EndNote—automates the collection, organization, and formatting of citations. These tools plug directly into word processors like Microsoft Word, generating in-text citations and compiling reference lists instantly in whichever style the nursing student selects, whether APA, Vancouver, or Harvard. While these applications save considerable time during large research projects, student nurses must remain vigilant. Automated tools frequently pull messy metadata from web scrapers, resulting in capitalized titles or missing publisher locations that require manual correction before final submission.
